root_cause.text: The netfilter x_tables TCP/DCCP option-walking code in `xt_tcpudp.c` and `xt_dccp.c` failed to validate that a length byte existed before using `op[i + 1]` for multi-byte options, causing an out-of-bounds 1-byte read when the final option byte was a non-single-byte kind.
root_cause.evidence: The CVE and commit message explicitly state that “when the last byte of options is a non-single-byte option kind, walkers that advance with `i += op[i + 1] ? : 1` can read `op[i + 1]` past the end of the option area,” and the patch fixes this by adding `|| i == optlen - 1` before dereferencing `op[i + 1]` in both `tcp_find_option()` and `dccp_find_option()`.

intent_record.intent_summary: Add a bounds check in dccp_find_option() to avoid reading past the end of the options buffer when parsing the final byte.
intent_record.what: The loop condition handling in dccp_find_option() was changed so that the single-byte advance case now triggers not only when op[i] < 2, but also when i == optlen - 1; the alternative branch remains functionally the same except for whitespace formatting in the expression i += op[i + 1] ? : 1.
intent_record.how: At runtime, this prevents the code from reading op[i + 1] when the parser is positioned at the last byte of the options buffer, avoiding an out-of-bounds access and safely advancing by one byte instead.

intent_record.intent_summary: Add a bounds check in tcp_find_option() to avoid accessing the option-length byte past the end of the TCP options buffer.
intent_record.what: The loop logic in tcp_find_option() was changed from a two-line conditional increment to a block that also checks whether the current index is at the last byte of the options buffer. Previously it advanced by one byte only when op[i] < 2; now it advances by one byte when op[i] < 2 or when i == optlen - 1, otherwise it advances by op[i + 1] ?: 1.
intent_record.how: This prevents the code from reading op[i + 1] when the parser is positioned at the final byte of the options buffer, avoiding an out-of-bounds access while still correctly advancing through malformed or truncated TCP option data.

bic_trace_step.reason: The function body is sufficient because it contains the full option-walking loop and the exact length-byte access. The vulnerable construct is present in the loop at lines 57-67: after handling single-byte options with `if (op[i] < 2) i++;`, the multi-byte case does `i += op[i+1]?:1;` (line 66). There is no prior check that `i + 1 < optlen` before reading `op[i+1]`. Therefore, if the last remaining byte in the options area is a non-single-byte option kind (`op[i] >= 2`), the code will read one byte past the end of the options buffer. The fix is not present because correct handling would validate that a length byte exists before using `op[i+1]`; no such bounds check appears anywhere in this function.

bic_trace_step.reason: The relevant logic is fully visible in `tcp_find_option()`, so the snippet is sufficient to assess the issue. The vulnerable construct is present in the loop: `for (i = 0; i < optlen; ) { if (op[i] == option) return !invert; if (op[i] < 2) i++; else i += op[i+1]?:1; }`. For multi-byte options (`op[i] >= 2`), the code reads `op[i+1]` as the length byte without first checking that `i + 1 < optlen`. If the final byte of the options area is a non-single-byte kind, this causes an out-of-bounds 1-byte read exactly matching the stated root cause. There is no guard such as `if (i + 1 >= optlen)` before dereferencing `op[i+1]`, so the fix is not present.
